title: Allowing up to four units on residential lots
subtitle: Also: a building-code limiting distance agreement for Benninger Drive townhouses and the 2023 growth monitoring report.
overview: The committee recommended that Council adopt city-initiated Official Plan and Zoning By-law changes allowing up to four dwelling units on lots that permit a single detached, semi-detached or street-townhouse dwelling {{vote:m2}}. Staff said about 11,000 more lots would become eligible. Smaller minimum lot sizes would apply in suburban areas, and parking rules would be relaxed near transit and in the central city. Detached additional units could be slightly taller.

An amendment asks staff to report back by fall 2025 on how many four-unit dwellings, including additional dwelling units, have been built. The committee noted the recommendation was to go to a Special Council meeting later the same day. Staff said the work is tied to the city's Housing Accelerator Fund commitments.

The committee also authorized a limiting distance agreement for stacked townhouses at 630 Benninger Dr {{vote:m1}}. It also agreed that the 2023 growth monitoring report will be used to meet the city's reporting obligation to the Region of Waterloo {{vote:m3}}.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended adopting the Official Plan amendment and Zoning By-law amendments for By-laws 85-1 and 2019-051 to permit up to four units on eligible lots, with a staff report back by fall 2025 on the number built.
The committee authorized the Mayor and Clerk to sign an agreement allowing five blocks of stacked townhouses to measure limiting distance onto the adjacent city stormwater pond block.

The committee agreed that the 2023 Kitchener Growth Management Strategy Annual Monitoring Report will be used to meet Clause 22.1 of the administrative agreement with the Region on delegated approval authority.

debate: A delegate supported the proposal but asked that green standards apply to new four-unit projects and renovations. The requests were electric heating and cooling instead of natural gas, permeable hard surfaces, and better transit and active transportation in newly intensified areas. Staff said these projects fall below the site plan control threshold, so such standards cannot be enforced. Staff suggested Council could advocate to the Province on Building Code changes.

Several councillors questioned the 10.5-metre minimum lot width in suburban areas and the limits on driveway widening. Staff said parking drives lot size and that wider driveways cut into boulevard space, utilities, snow storage and street trees. Staff offered to look at how many more lots a narrower width would enable, and said minor variances remain available for unusual lots.

Some councillors were concerned about protecting neighbours' mature trees. Staff said damage to trees on neighbouring property is a civil matter, but a separate tree conservation by-law review is under way. One councillor said the city should have aligned the two efforts.

Several councillors wanted the units to be easier to own, not just rent, and said the triplex lot width of 13.1 metres may have held back uptake. Staff said the new regulations would lower lot sizes for triplexes and detached additional units too. They said freehold or condominium ownership is not prohibited but is harder to set up. Councillors also raised financing barriers and asked for advocacy.

A councillor read resident comments opposing the change, citing property values, crime and strain on services. The Chair cautioned about the tone of some of the comments. Staff said change can be hard for neighbourhoods and that earlier changes to allow duplexes, triplexes and detached additional units had seen modest uptake.
